# **Mathematical Modeling and Architectural Replication of Empirical Driving Performance Metrics in WebGL Virtual Environments**

## **Operational Definitions and Taxonomic Classification of Primary Driving Performance Metrics**

Driving performance metrics in empirical research are classified into control-level inputs and maneuvering-level outputs1. Control-level inputs signify the immediate cybernetic interactions of the driver with the vehicle's interfaces, primarily encompassing steering wheel adjustments, throttle modulation, and braking responses2. Maneuvering-level outputs capture the resultant closed-loop trajectory of the vehicle relative to the physical geometry of the roadway, manifesting as speed variations, lateral lane deviations, and temporal or spatial safety margins1.  
In cognitive psychology, pharmacology, and automotive safety engineering, these metrics serve as highly sensitive indicators of driver state degradation4. Empirical studies utilize vehicle control metrics to quantify the impact of sleep deprivation, central nervous system depressants, alcohol consumption, and secondary cognitive or visual workloads on a driver's operational capacity4. By continuously recording longitudinal and lateral control variables, researchers can dissect the exact mechanisms through which attention lapses, psychomotor slowing, or physical drowsiness compromise vehicle stability and increase crash risks7.

| Metric | Level of Control | Primary Operational Variable | Cognitive/Physiological Sensitivity | Data Capture Frequency | Foundational References |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SDLP** | Maneuvering Output | Lateral distance relative to lane centerline (![][image1]) | Sedation, alcohol intoxication, sleep deprivation, visual distraction4. | 2 Hz to 10 Hz7. | O'Hanlon (1984); Verster et al. (2011)4 |
| **SDS** | Maneuvering Output | Forward vehicle speed (![][image2]) | Vigilance decrements, monotonous road layout, arousal states1. | 2 Hz to 10 Hz7. | O'Hanlon (1984); Verster et al. (2011)7 |
| **SWRR** | Control Input | Steering wheel angle (![][image3]) | Secondary cognitive task load, visual off-road glances15. | 10 Hz to 100 Hz15. | Markkula & Engström (2006)8 |
| **SE (![][image4])** | Control Input | Steering wheel prediction error (![][image5]) | Subtle attention shifts, microsleep episodes, cognitive load14. | 6.67 Hz to 9.6 Hz14. | Nakayama et al. (1999); Boer (2000)19 |
| **TLC (![][image6])** | Maneuvering Output | Vehicle boundary-crossing trajectory | Lane keeping safety margins, hazard neglect, sleep apnea1. | 10 Hz to 100 Hz18. | Godthelp (1984); van Winsum et al. (2000)1 |

## **Mathematical Formulation of Core Evaluation Metrics**

### **Standard Deviation of Lateral Position**

The Standard Deviation of Lateral Position (SDLP) is universally regarded as the experimental gold standard for assessing vehicle lateral control stability and road-tracking error4. Physically representing the amplitude of vehicle "weaving" or tracking deviation within a traffic lane, SDLP is calculated by taking the standard deviation of the vehicle's lateral coordinate relative to the lane centerline over a continuous driving segment4.  
Mathematically, if ![][image1] represents the lateral displacement of the vehicle's center of gravity relative to the lane centerline at discrete sample ![][image7], and ![][image8] represents the total number of samples collected, the formulation of SDLP is expressed as:  
![][image9]  
where the Mean Lateral Position (MLP) is defined as:  
![][image10]  
In historical pharmacological and toxicological studies, SDLP has been calibrated against incremental blood alcohol concentrations (BAC) to define standardized thresholds of driving impairment4. The highway driving test is traditionally performed in actual traffic on a 100 km segment with instructions to maintain a steady lane position and a constant speed of 95 km/h4. Under these conditions, the baseline placebo SDLP remains highly stable across individuals7.

| Impairment Condition / Drug State | Equivalent Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) | Expected Increase in SDLP (ΔSDLP) | Cognitive/Physiological Mechanisms | Standard Segment Chunking |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Placebo / Rested Baseline** | **![][image11]** | **![][image12]** (Reference) | Uncompromised sensorimotor loop and alert tracking4. | 100 km or 3 km intervals7. |
| **Legal Limit Threshold (Social Drinking)** | **![][image13]** | **![][image14]** to ![][image15] | Initial deterioration of fine motor coordination and spatial tracking4. | 3 km rural segments13. |
| **Moderate Alcohol Impairment** | **![][image16]** | **![][image17]** | Significant delay in corrective tracking and spatial margin perception4. | 3 km rural segments4. |
| **Severe Alcohol Impairment** | **![][image18]** | **![][image19]** | Slowed reflexes, diminished motor control, and visual tracking failure4. | 3 km rural segments4. |
| **Zuranolone Sedation (50 mg, Day 2\)** | \~ ![][image16] equivalent | ![][image20] (LSM difference) | Central nervous system depression, slower processing speed10. | 3 km rural segments10. |
| **Zuranolone Sedation (100 mg, Day 8\)** | Exceeds ![][image21] equivalent | ![][image22] (LSM difference) | Extended attention lapses, profound motor execution delay4. | 3 km rural segments10. |
| **Sleep Deprivation (Overnight)** | Variable | ![][image23] (On-Road) to ![][image24] (Simulator) | Micro-sleep occurrences, structural breakdown of tracking control5. | 3 km rural segments5. |

The significant difference in sleep deprivation effects between simulated driving (![][image24]) and real-world highway driving (![][image23]) highlights a critical structural discrepancy in simulator validity5. Under sleep deprivation, the correlation between simulator performance and real-world performance drops from ![][image25] (well-rested) to a non-significant ![][image26]5.  
This decoupling indicates that simulators amplify tracking errors when biological arousal is low, likely because the real-world physical risk of collision enforces a compensatory focus that is absent in a virtual environment5.  
Furthermore, eye-tracking integration reveals that lateral control instability correlates with gaze variables24. Reduced percentage of time focused on the road center, lower standard deviation of eye opening, and narrowed horizontal gaze directly predict elevated SDLP values, demonstrating the deep coupling between spatial visual scanning and lateral coordinate preservation24.

### **Standard Deviation of Speed**

The Standard Deviation of Speed (SDS) captures the longitudinal control variability of the vehicle, serving as an index of the driver's ability to maintain a steady velocity profile2. While SDLP assesses lateral "weaving" across the lane boundaries, SDS quantifies longitudinal stability under task demands7.  
If ![][image2] represents the forward velocity of the vehicle at discrete sample ![][image7], and ![][image8] represents the total number of samples collected, the formulation of SDS is expressed as:  
![][image27]  
where the Mean Speed (MS) is defined as:  
![][image28]  
Although SDS measures vehicle control, drug-induced or cognitive impairment is less clearly observed in this metric than in lateral weaving7. Speed variability usually has fewer immediate consequences for traffic safety than weaving of the car7. However, under severe sleep deprivation or clinical depression, SDS increases significantly due to micro-sleeps or central nervous system slowing, resulting in larger, erratic adjustments to the accelerator pedal12.  
In specialized research environments, SDS is paired with a Speeding Index—which weighs the proportion of the drive exceeding the speed limit by the magnitude of speeding—to evaluate risk adaptation strategies in non-optimal states13.

### **Steering Wheel Reversal Rate**

The Steering Wheel Reversal Rate (SWRR) measures the frequency of directional changes in the steering wheel angle that exceed a specified angular threshold, reflecting the driver's corrective effort and cognitive workload15. Smooth driving relies on continuous, low-amplitude anticipatory steering adjustments19.  
When cognitive or visual secondary tasks divert attention, this continuous loop is disrupted, leading to delayed, abrupt corrective actions that increase SWRR15.  
The SWRR calculation is parameterized by a "gap size" or angular threshold (![][image29])15. The standard computational algorithm proposed by Markkula and Engström involves three consecutive stages15:

1. **Signal Conditioning**: A low-pass filter (typically a second-order digital Butterworth filter with a cutoff frequency ![][image30] between ![][image31] and ![][image32]) is applied to the raw steering wheel angle signal ![][image33] to eliminate high-frequency mechanical noise and digitization jitter15.  
2. **Stationary Point Detection**: For the conditioned sequence of steering angles ![][image3] sampled at uniform intervals, an approximation of the first-order derivative is evaluated. A stationary point (local extremum) is identified at index ![][image7] if the sign of the local slope reverses15:  
   ![][image34]  
3. **Reversal Counting**: Extrema are filtered to isolate significant directional changes. Let the sequence of temporal sorted extrema be ![][image35]. An upward reversal is registered if the steering angle increases from a local minimum to a subsequent local maximum such that15:  
   ![][image36]  
   Conversely, a downward reversal is registered when moving from a maximum to a minimum where the absolute reduction equals or exceeds ![][image29]15.

| Gap Parameter (θgap​) | Reversal Type Classification | Target Cognitive / Visual State Sensitivity | Expected Behavioral Outcome | Primary References |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **![][image37] to ![][image38]** | Micro-Reversals15 | High cognitive workload, auditory processing, working memory tasks15. | Elevated rate of rapid, minor manual adjustments to maintain central lane placement15. | Markkula & Engström (2006); Kujala et al. (2018)15 |
| ![][image39] **to ![][image40]** | Macro-Reversals15 | Visual distraction, off-road glances, texting, mobile phone interactions15. | Abrupt, large-amplitude corrective inputs following spatial drift during glances14. | Markkula & Engström (2006); Perez et al. (2024)15 |
| ![][image41] **to ![][image42]** | Rapid Steering Wheel Movements (RSWM)26 | Highly critical near-crash events, collision avoidance maneuvers, emergency response26. | Violent, extreme steering wheel inputs executed to prevent run-off-the-road or impact26. | Ranney et al. (2011); Yuka Bounding Volume Documentation26 |

SWRR can also be contrasted with the High Frequency Component of steering angle (HFC), which is calculated by applying a Fourier transform to the steering profile to determine the ratio of power between ![][image43] and ![][image44] relative to the entire steering spectrum26.  
HFC isolates pure correction dynamics from low-frequency open-loop steering, serving as a direct representation of driver workload across both straight paths and complex curve-following scenarios26.

### **Steering Entropy**

Steering Entropy (SE) is an information-theoretic metric designed to quantify the randomness, discontinuity, and unpredictability of a driver's control inputs14. Developed by Nakayama et al. and optimized by Boer, the metric is constructed around the principle that a driver's steering profile during unconstrained, undistracted conditions is highly predictable via second-order kinematic extrapolation14.  
When physical or cognitive capacity is compromised, the proportion of unexpected, high-frequency corrective maneuvers increases, causing the prediction error distribution to widen20.  
To calculate steering entropy, the steering wheel angle signal is first downsampled to a frequency reflecting the baseline of human motor control limits, typically ![][image45], ![][image46], or ![][image47]14. At each sample index ![][image48], a predicted steering wheel angle ![][image49] is generated using a second-order Taylor expansion based on the three preceding physical samples14:  
![][image50]  
The prediction error ![][image51] is calculated as the absolute difference between the actual and predicted steering angle14:  
![][image52]  
Under baseline driving conditions (minimum mental workload, straight road geometries, rested state), a reference distribution of ![][image51] is constructed14. A scale parameter, ![][image53], is determined from this baseline distribution, representing the 90th percentile of prediction errors14. Mathematically, ![][image53] corresponds to ![][image54] standard deviations of the baseline prediction error distribution, ensuring that 90% of normal driving errors fall within the interval ![][image55]19.  
The prediction error distribution is partitioned into nine discrete bins, indexed from ![][image56] to ![][image57], defined symmetrically around ![][image53] as follows14:

| Bin Index | Mathematical Boundary Range | Expected Probability Distribution (Baseline) | Interpretation under Elevated Impairment / Workload |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Bin 1** | **![][image58]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] (Extremely Rare) | Extreme corrective steering input to the right14. |
| **Bin 2** | **![][image60]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] (Rare) | Large amplitude corrective adjustment14. |
| **Bin 3** | **![][image61]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] | Minor corrective steering input to the right14. |
| **Bin 4** | **![][image62]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] | Small directional drift error19. |
| **Bin 5** | **![][image63]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] (Dominant Mode) | Highly smooth, predictable tracking19. |
| **Bin 6** | **![][image64]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] | Small directional drift error19. |
| **Bin 7** | **![][image65]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] | Minor corrective steering input to the left14. |
| **Bin 8** | **![][image66]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] (Rare) | Large amplitude corrective adjustment14. |
| **Bin 9** | **![][image67]** \[cite: 14, 19\] | ![][image59] (Extremely Rare) | Extreme corrective steering input to the left14. |

During experimental trials, the probability ![][image68] of prediction errors falling into each of these nine bins is computed14. The Steering Entropy (![][image4]) is then calculated by applying Shannon's entropy formula to the probability vector14:  
![][image69]  
For baseline driving, the prediction errors remain concentrated in the central bin, resulting in low entropy values (typically ![][image70] to ![][image71])14. Under intense secondary task distraction, sleepiness, or neurological impairment, the error distribution spreads into the outer bins, causing ![][image4] to rise significantly (often exceeding ![][image72])14.  
To classify driver cognitive conditions in real-time, studies use quantile discretization of steering entropy34. Threshold limits are set to classify cognitive state into three functional brackets: small cognitive load (![][image73]), medium cognitive load (![][image74]), and high cognitive load (![][image75])34.  
While the Taylor expansion provides a robust, standardized mathematical platform, Boer (2000) proposed an alternative approach replacing the Taylor series with a prediction filter derived from an Autoregressive (AR) model of the reference baseline steering data20.  
Because the AR filter is tuned to the specific frequency spectral signatures of individual drivers, it offers higher sensitivity when analyzing subtle tracking deviations under complex roadway geometries20.

### **Time-to-Line Crossing**

Time-to-Line Crossing (TLC) is a continuous safety margin metric that represents the temporal duration remaining before any part of the vehicle's perimeter crosses a boundary of the travel lane, assuming the vehicle proceeds along its projected trajectory under its current state1. Unlike distance-based metrics, TLC integrates lateral position, longitudinal speed, heading angle, and steering inputs into a single dynamic safety index2.  
A first-order, lateral-velocity-based approximation of TLC is occasionally utilized in basic collision warning architectures due to its minimal sensing requirements2:  
![][image76]  
where ![][image77] is the lateral distance from the outer tire sidewall to the nearest lane boundary, and ![][image78] is the vehicle's lateral velocity vector relative to the lane2. This linear approximation assumes a constant lateral velocity, which is physically unrealistic during continuous driving where drivers weave or negotiate curves2.  
Consequently, this approximation produces highly unstable, fluctuating TLC values that tend toward infinity as the vehicle's heading aligns parallel to the lane (making ![][image78] approach zero)2.  
For high-fidelity research, a trigonometric method is required9. In a straight road scenario, assuming a vehicle with a relative yaw angle (heading error) ![][image79] and a constant forward velocity ![][image80], the time to cross the left or right boundary is computed using:  
![][image81]  
where ![][image82] represents the immediate perpendicular distance from the outer tire boundary to the respective lane marker36.  
On curved roadways or when the vehicle is traversing a curved path (with a non-zero steering angle), the path must be modeled as a circular arc of radius ![][image83]36. If ![][image82] is the lateral distance to the boundary line, and ![][image79] is the relative yaw angle to the tangent of the curve, the trigonometric TLC equation is formulated as:  
![][image84]  
In curved road sections, a highly detailed geometric relationship is formulated by integrating vehicle dimensions, dynamic slip angles, and road curvature parameters36. Let ![][image85] represent the radius of curvature of the road lane boundary and ![][image86] represent the immediate lateral displacement of the vehicle center of gravity36.  
When the front wheels steering angle ![][image87] is non-zero, the front tires' relative yaw angle is established as ![][image88]36. The distance along the projected circular vehicle path to the line crossing boundary (![][image89]) is solved using the quadratic cosine rule36:  
![][image90]  
Dividing the resulting distance to line crossing (![][image89]) by the vehicle's forward velocity (![][image80]) generates the dynamic TLC value36.  
Because TLC is a continuous signal that exhibits highly skewed distributions during stable driving, researchers rarely analyze mean values1. Instead, they compute the minimum TLC value over a segment—representing the critical threshold of hazard exposure—or the 15th percentile of TLC (![][image6]), which serves as a highly robust proxy for the driver's accepted lateral safety margin1.

## **Technical Adaptation and Replication in Three.js and WebGL Systems**

Replicating these research metrics inside a browser-based simulator constructed with Three.js requires addressing several challenges unique to client-side JavaScript execution, such as variable execution frame rates, garbage collection pauses, and coordinate system projections38.

### **Deterministic Frame Decoupling and Physics Loop**

To ensure that statistical metrics (such as downsampled steering entropy and Butterworth low-pass filters) are calculated with high mathematical validity, the simulator must operate on a deterministic, uniform sampling rate39. Relying on the variable delta time (![][image91]) provided directly by browser-based frame rendering events (via requestAnimationFrame) introduces sampling artifacts that distort frequency-dependent calculations39.  
The physical update loop is decoupled from the rendering loop using an accumulator pattern39. This ensures that the vehicle kinematic state is updated at a fixed interval (e.g., ![][image92] or ![][image93]), while rendering scales dynamically to match high-refresh-rate displays39.  
To eliminate visual stutter or high-frequency jitter resulting from this decoupling, visual transforms of the vehicle and camera are linearly interpolated (lerp) using the fractional remainder of the physics accumulator40:

JavaScript  
class SimulationLoop {  
  constructor(updateCallback, renderCallback, physicsHz \= 100) {  
    this.update \= updateCallback;  
    this.render \= renderCallback;  
    this.dt \= 1.0 / physicsHz; // Fixed physics step (0.01s)  
    this.accumulator \= 0.0;  
    this.lastTime \= 0.0;  
    this.currentState \= { pos: new THREE.Vector3(), rot: new THREE.Quaternion() };  
    this.previousState \= { pos: new THREE.Vector3(), rot: new THREE.Quaternion() };  
  }

  tick(currentTime) {  
    if (this.lastTime \=== 0) {  
      this.lastTime \= currentTime;  
      requestAnimationFrame((t) \=\> this.tick(t));  
      return;  
    }

    const frameTime \= (currentTime \- this.lastTime) / 1000.0;  
    this.lastTime \= currentTime;

    // Cap frame time to prevent performance drops from lagging the simulation  
    const maxFrameTime \= 0.25;  
    this.accumulator \+= Math.min(frameTime, maxFrameTime);

    while (this.accumulator \>= this.dt) {  
      // Archive state for interpolation  
      this.previousState.pos.copy(this.currentState.pos);  
      this.previousState.rot.copy(this.currentState.rot);

      // Execute deterministic update  
      this.update(this.dt, this.currentState);  
      this.accumulator \-= this.dt;  
    }

    // Compute interpolation blend factor alpha  
    const alpha \= this.accumulator / this.dt;  
    this.render(alpha, this.previousState, this.currentState);

    requestAnimationFrame((t) \=\> this.tick(t));  
  }  
}

### **Real-Time Lateral Error Projection onto Splines**

In a Three.js environment, the centerlines and physical boundaries of roadways are typically represented mathematically by three-dimensional parametric curves, such as THREE.CatmullRomCurve345. Calculating the lateral tracking error ![][image1] for SDLP requires projecting the vehicle's position vector onto the curve to locate the closest point48.  
Using a fine-grained, equi-distance sampling approach across the spline curve provides high spatial resolution50. By pre-computing a high-density polyline segment representation of the road spline, the minimum distance is calculated using localized orthogonal projections without the overhead of real-time parameter solvers48.  
The coordinate projection onto the line segment formed by vertices ![][image94] and ![][image95] identifies the closest projected point ![][image96] using the dot product49:  
![][image97]  
The projection parameter is clamped to ![][image98] to ensure the point resides within the physical boundaries of the local segment49.

JavaScript  
class SplineTracker {  
  constructor(catmullSpline, segmentCount \= 1000) {  
    this.curve \= catmullSpline;  
    // Generate high-density spatial coordinates  
    this.points \= this.curve.getSpacedPoints(segmentCount);  
      
    // Allocate scratchpad variables to avoid garbage collection overhead  
    this.carProj \= new THREE.Vector3();  
    this.segDir \= new THREE.Vector3();  
    this.carToSegStart \= new THREE.Vector3();  
    this.roadNormal \= new THREE.Vector3();  
    this.upVector \= new THREE.Vector3(0, 1, 0);  
  }

  calculateLateralOffset(carPos) {  
    let minD2 \= Infinity;  
    let closestIdx \= 0;

    // Spatial broad-phase: identify nearest vertex index  
    for (let i \= 0; i \< this.points.length; i++) {  
      const d2 \= carPos.distanceToSquared(this.points\[i\]);  
      if (d2 \< minD2) {  
        minD2 \= d2;  
        closestIdx \= i;  
      }  
    }

    // Determine segment bounds for localized projection  
    const idx0 \= closestIdx \=== 0 ? 0 : closestIdx \- 1;  
    const idx1 \= closestIdx \=== this.points.length \- 1 ? closestIdx : closestIdx \+ 1;  
      
    const p0 \= this.points\[idx0\];  
    const p1 \= this.points\[idx1\];

    // Orthogonal vector projection  
    this.segDir.subVectors(p1, p0);  
    const segLenSq \= this.segDir.lengthSq();  
      
    this.carToSegStart.subVectors(carPos, p0);  
    let t \= this.carToSegStart.dot(this.segDir) / segLenSq;  
    t \= Math.max(0.0, Math.min(1.0, t)); // Clamp to segment boundaries

    this.carProj.copy(this.segDir).multiplyScalar(t).add(p0);

    // Compute signed tracking error  
    const distance \= carPos.distanceTo(this.carProj);  
      
    // Construct local normal frame from road tangent  
    this.segDir.normalize(); // Now acts as road tangent vector  
    this.roadNormal.crossVectors(this.segDir, this.upVector).normalize();

    const signedDot \= this.carToSegStart.dot(this.roadNormal);  
    const signedOffset \= distance \* Math.sign(signedDot);

    return {  
      signedOffset: signedOffset, // In meters (positive \= left, negative \= right)  
      projectedPoint: this.carProj.clone(),  
      tangent: this.segDir.clone()  
    };  
  }  
}

### **High-Fidelity Spatial Volume Collision via Oriented Bounding Boxes**

To execute mathematically robust boundary crossing detections and determine precise Time-to-Line Crossing (TLC) limits, the vehicle footprint must be represented as a three-dimensional oriented volume rather than a point source2. In Three.js, this is achieved using the OBB (Oriented Bounding Box) mathematical class51.

JavaScript  
import { OBB } from 'three/addons/math/OBB.js';

class VehicleVolumeTracker {  
  constructor(vehicleWidth, vehicleLength, vehicleHeight) {  
    this.halfSize \= new THREE.Vector3(vehicleWidth / 2, vehicleHeight / 2, vehicleLength / 2);  
    this.localOBB \= new OBB(new THREE.Vector3(), this.halfSize, new THREE.Matrix3());  
    this.worldOBB \= new OBB();  
  }

  update(mesh) {  
    // Synchronize spatial volume transformations with the rendering mesh  
    this.worldOBB.copy(this.localOBB);  
    this.worldOBB.applyMatrix4(mesh.matrixWorld);  
  }

  checkBoundaryCrossing(laneBoundaryPlane) {  
    // Immediate mathematical intersection verification  
    return this.worldOBB.intersectsPlane(laneBoundaryPlane);  
  }  
    
  checkCollision(obstacleOBB) {  
    // OBB-to-OBB intersection based on the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT)  
    return this.worldOBB.intersectsOBB(obstacleOBB);  
  }  
}

By leveraging these geometric verification systems, researchers can construct a programmatic pipeline to analyze the safety margins of lane keeping9.  
When the vehicle's spatial volume encroaches on or intersects the road boundaries, the physical intersection point is projected back to the coordinate plane using orthogonal mapping52. This maps the spatial deviation to an exact value in the tracking data series51.

## **Synthesis of Cognitive-Behavioral Driving Signatures**

A multi-dimensional approach reveals that changes in driving performance under altered biological states are rarely uniform; instead, they are characterized by adaptive behavioral strategies and compensatory tradeoffs23.  
When drivers experience high mental workload (e.g., performing a secondary cognitive task), they often display a paradox of narrower lateral tracking, resulting in *decreased* SDLP9. However, analyzing this state alongside control inputs and safety margins exposes a highly active, closed-loop compensation process9.  
This compensatory pattern is identified by a dramatic rise in micro-steering wheel reversals (![][image99] to ![][image38]) and elevated Steering Entropy (![][image4]), as the driver executes a continuous sequence of rapid, minor adjustments to counter lateral drifting9.  
This high level of effort leads to a simultaneous reduction in the temporal safety margin (TLC), exposing the driver to extreme risk if a sudden longitudinal hazard requires an immediate steering or braking response9.  
Conversely, sleepiness, pharmacological sedation, and alcohol impairment produce a completely different cognitive-behavioral signature4. Under diminished arousal, the open-loop phase of driving expands, causing the driver to neglect spatial tracking errors and drift slowly toward the lane boundaries1.  
This state is characterized by a drop in micro-reversal rates, extremely low TLC values, and elevated SDS (speed variation)1.  
When the vehicle eventually reaches the lane boundary, the driver executes an abrupt, large-amplitude steering adjustment, which registers as a sharp increase in macro-reversals (![][image100]), elevated SDLP, and high Steering Entropy (![][image4])4.

| Behavioral Driver State | SDLP Trend | Steering Entropy (Hp​) | Micro-Reversals (0.5∘−2.0∘) | Macro-Reversals (≥2.5∘) | TLC Margin (TLC15th​) | Adaptive / Compensatory Strategy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **High Cognitive Workload** | Decreased9 | Elevated19 | Significantly Increased15 | Unchanged / Low15 | Consistently Decreased9 | Compensatory: active micro-corrections prevent drift but deplete spare mental capacity9. |
| **Monotonous Fatigue / Drowsiness** | Significantly Increased5 | High (Erratic Profile)14 | Decreased1 | Significantly Increased14 | Severely Reduced1 | Maladaptive: open-loop drift punctuated by sudden, late steering overcorrections14. |
| **Sedation / Alcohol (BAC ![][image101])** | Significantly Increased4 | Elevated19 | Decreased4 | Increased4 | Severely Reduced1 | Systemic psychomotor slowing: delayed reaction times and degraded motor coordination4. |

## **Conclusions**

Integrating these findings into virtual architectures demonstrates that evaluating driving performance requires a holistic, multi-dimensional tracking framework6. Using SDLP in isolation to assess vehicle stability can lead to misleading conclusions, as narrower lateral tracking can mask a highly distracted or cognitively overloaded driver9.  
A robust evaluation platform must analyze lateral coordinate weaving (SDLP) alongside steering input dynamics (SWRR, Steering Entropy) and continuous temporal safety margins (TLC)2.  
Decoupling the physics loop from the rendering engine, applying recursive digital filtering, and implementing oriented bounding volumes for real-time spatial checks allows browser-based Three.js simulators to replicate these standardized human factors metrics with high scientific and statistical validity39.
